title: Athabaskan migration to the Southwest
summary: Athabaskan-speaking ancestors of the Navajo and Apache migrated south from Canada’s Mackenzie Basin into the American Southwest. Scholars disagree on timing: some say the southward move began about 1000 and ended by the early 1500s, while Crow Canyon says they probably arrived after A.D. 1450 and were in the Mesa Verde region by the early 1500s. The groups later split into the Navajo and the Apache.

uncertainty.note: EBSCO Research Starters says most scholars put the start of the southward move about 1000 and its end in the early 1500s; Crow Canyon says arrival after A.D. 1450. The id year 1300 follows neither source and is not used.

beats.caption: Athabaskan speakers begin moving south from Canada’s Mackenzie Basin, according to most scholars cited by EBSCO.
Crow Canyon says they probably reached the Southwest after A.D. 1450, and Mesa Verde by the early 1500s.
Once in the Southwest, the groups differentiated into the Navajo and Apache peoples.

reviewer_note: Least sure: dating is openly contested between the sources (start about 1000 vs arrival after 1450), so the span is wide and confidence is contested. The Mackenzie Basin point is an anchor (Great Slave Lake from Wikidata), not a sourced site; uncertainty 1500 km. The id year 1300 is not supported by either source.
